intro: Painters gave figures and objects a sense of place through changes in light, weight, receding space and surface detail. These four treatments include overlapping categories.
alt: Four Renaissance-inspired painting studies. A figure appears on a gold ground, in detailed oil interiors and among a pyramidal group.

variants.name: Proto-Renaissance
variants.look: A weighty figure and a ledge suggest shallow space against a field of gold.
variants.history: Italian painters around 1300, including Giotto, explored ways to give figures volume and make narrative scenes spatially clear.
variants.when: Look here when you need to show a figure that can carry an object or lean into another figure while retaining a stylized setting.
variants.why: A few coherent changes of light and weight are enough for the viewer to imagine a body under cloth.

variants.name: Early Netherlandish painting
variants.look: Oil-painted highlights pick out the edges of objects and the sheen of a polished vessel.
variants.history: In the fifteenth-century Low Countries, painters refined layered oil techniques for works that included portraits, altarpieces and devotional panels.
variants.when: Study how a small reflected highlight can set the scale and material of an object.
variants.why: Thin paint layers can give a small image dark depth and sharp surface detail at the same time.

variants.name: Northern Renaissance
variants.look: The eye can move from carefully depicted objects in an indoor setting to the brighter landscape beyond.
variants.history: Renaissance art north of the Alps varied across regions and overlapped with Early Netherlandish painting. Its artists developed sophisticated work in oils, drawing and prints.
variants.when: Study the way a single view can reward close inspection and still suggest a world outside the room.
variants.why: Specific textures help establish the foreground, while light and distance pull the eye farther through the picture.

variants.name: High Renaissance
variants.look: The people and the landscape are held in a balanced composition with overlapping forms and softened distance.
variants.history: The High Renaissance usually refers to a period of Italian Renaissance art around the turn of the sixteenth century, associated with artists including Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo.
variants.when: Study a many-figure composition when gestures need to lead toward a shared visual center.
variants.why: Grouping the biggest shapes into a simple structure makes individual faces and actions easier to locate.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: Italian Proto-Renaissance figure study: panel painting with gilded ground, weighty draped seated figure and shallow spatial platform, compare conventions transparently; Early Netherlandish: tiny oil-glazed portrait by a polished brass vessel and sharp lace texture in shadowed room; Northern Renaissance: room adjoining an open luminous landscape, finely delineated woven textile, crystal and small cut flowers; High Renaissance: unified pyramidal grouping of figures in calm and atmospheric idealized landscape with softened edges. Repaint the recurring woman in the idiom where possible, never as a real past person. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
